# Concave homothetic profiles: exact projective coordinates and a scalar-anchor obstruction

This note investigates a possible extension of `candidate 2be89ee8039bb5fd`. It proves exact coordinate and coarea identities, then gives an exact obstruction to retaining the pyramid's particular scalar correction unchanged. It does not refute another scalar correction or the stationary-menu inequality.

## 1. The actual body and its projective axial coordinate

Let D be a centrally symmetric m-dimensional convex body centered at zero, m>=1. Let r be a positive concave function on a compact interval [a,b], where a<0<b. Put d=m+1 and

    K={(X,z):a<=z<=b, X in r(z)D}.

For the differential formulas first assume r is C2; positive piecewise affine concave profiles satisfy the same formulas almost everywhere, which suffices for every integral below. Define

    u=z/r(z),    R(u)=1/r(z(u)),    D_r(z)=r(z)-z r'(z).

Concavity and positivity at zero imply D_r(z)>=r(0)>0. Consequently u is strictly increasing, with

    du/dz=D_r/r^2,      dz/du=r^2/D_r,
    R'=-r'/D_r,        R''=-r^3 r''/D_r^3>=0.        (1)

In particular R is convex. For a piecewise affine r, R is continuous piecewise affine and convex; (1) on each piece and the monotonicity of its one-sided slopes prove this directly. Also

    R-uR'=1/D_r>0.

The actual change of variables X=r(z)q, q in D, turns volume on K into product base volume dq and scalar axial density

    w(u)=(R-uR')R^(-d-1)=r(z(u))^(d+1)/D_r(z(u)).  (2)

Thus V_K=|D| int_I w(u)du, where I is the transformed axial interval. Extend w by zero outside I when writing integrals on all of D.

## 2. Caps and individual centroidal sections

Fix a raw continuous normal N=(c,1) and the through-zero cap

    H_c={z+c.X>=0}.

In the product coordinates its capture condition is exactly u+c.q>=0, so

    |K intersect H_c|
       =int_D int_{u>=-c.q} w(u)du dq.                (3)

On the section, u=-c.q. The raw coarea measure has base-coordinate density

    w(-c.q)R(-c.q) dq,                              (4)

where the expression is zero if -c.q is outside I. To check (4), before projectivizing use the delta/coarea factor for

    z+r(z)c.q.

Its derivative at the section is D_r/r>0, so volume Jacobian r^m gives coarea r^(m+1)/D_r=wR. The same formula follows by parameterizing the section as a graph over its projection and applying the ordinary graph Jacobian. Breakpoints of a piecewise affine profile affect only null base slices when c is nonzero. For c=0, the formula at u=0 is independent of the one-sided slope because R-uR'=R there.

Since X=q/R on the section, its horizontal first moment is

    int_D q w(-c.q)dq.                               (5)

The vertical first moment then vanishes automatically whenever (5) does, because z=-c.X on the section. Therefore the section centroid is zero exactly when

    int_D q w(-c.q)dq=0.                            (6)

The section has positive coarea for proper through-zero caps because zero is interior to K.

## 3. A genuine nonnegative coarea defect

Let L(u) be any affine support to the convex function R at zero. If (6) holds, integration cancels its linear term and gives

    int_D w(-c.q)R(-c.q)dq
       =R(0) int_D w(-c.q)dq + J_c,

    J_c:=int_D w(-c.q)[R(-c.q)-L(-c.q)]dq >=0.     (7)

For a single affine profile r, its projective reciprocal R is affine and J_c=0. That equality is the exact affine feature used by the pyramid's common scalar calculation. For genuinely nonaffine r, (7) retains the additional cost instead of identifying it with zero.

This does not yet give a favorable sign in the response-weighted cap budget: the scalar multiplying signed coarea can have either sign, and the two cap orientations reverse its sign. No cancellation or payment of J_c is asserted.

## 4. Exact failure of the same horizontal-anchored pyramid correction

Already in d=2, let r be the concave piecewise affine function with graph vertices

    (-5,5),  (-4,11),  (2,12).

Its two slopes are 6 and 1/6, so it is concave and positive. Let

    K={(x,z):-5<=z<=2, |x|<=r(z)}.

The area is

    V_K=2[8+69]=154,

and r(0)=35/3. The horizontal apex-oriented cap {z>=0} has fraction and normalized raw coarea

    p_0=71/231,    C_0=(2r(0))/154=35/231.

Consider the oblique cap

    H={z+(3/17)x>=0}.

Its section is exactly the segment with endpoints

    (34/3,-2),    (-34/3,2).

The first endpoint is on a sloping side, while the second is on the actual top facet z=2. Their midpoint is zero, so this is an actual centroidal proper section. Convexity and the direct section equation verify that these are the full chord endpoints, not just two selected points on the cutting line.

For -2<=z<=2 the captured interval length is

    r(z)+(17/3)z = 35/3+(35/6)z.

Below -2 the cap is empty, and there is no body above 2. Thus

    p=|K intersect H|/154=10/33,
    C= [section length/|(3/17,1)|]/154=34/231,
    e=C/C_0=34/35.

The specific scalar prescribed by the pyramid formula is

    c_*=(p_0-4/9)/C_0=-19/21.

Its corrected fraction is

    p-c_* C=2116/4851
           =4/9-40/4851 <4/9.                       (8)

Consequently an arbitrary positive-horizontal anchor at 4/9 fails for a nonaffine concave homothetic profile. There is an important orientation qualification: the local slope at zero here is positive, so the local virtual pyramid apex is toward NEGATIVE z. This first example alone does not refute a rule that always uses the local virtual-apex orientation. Its whole oblique section lies in the affine segment -4<=z<=2, so J_c in (7) is zero; this is only a warning that an arbitrary horizontal anchoring cannot be repaired using that section defect alone.

## 5. The virtual-apex orientation also fails in a nonaffine profile

For a counterexample retaining the virtual-apex orientation, take instead the concave profile with graph vertices

    (-5,5),  (-3,9),  (-1,12),  (3,10).

Its slopes are 2, 3/2 and -1/2. Near zero it is r(z)=23/2-z/2, whose virtual apex is at z=23, in the POSITIVE-z direction. The body has area

    V_K=2(14+21+44)=158,

and horizontal cap data

    p_0=129/316,   C_0=23/158.

The positive-z cap H={z+x/3>=0} has the actual centered chord with endpoints (9,-3),(-9,3). The lower endpoint is a side vertex, and the upper endpoint lies on the top facet, whose half-width is ten. Convexity gives the entire chord and excludes extension beyond either endpoint. Its capture is empty below -3. On [-3,3] its interval length is r(z)+3z, whose odd linear term integrates to zero. Therefore

    p=65/158,    C=18/158,    e=C/C_0=18/23.

The virtual-apex-oriented horizontal scalar is

    c_*=(p_0-4/9)/C_0=-103/414.

Nevertheless,

    p-c_*C=799/1817
            =4/9-77/16353 <4/9.                     (9)

Thus the particular pyramid scalar does not extend even when its orientation is inherited from the local affine profile at the source. Both certificates retain actual individual section centroids and an actual convex body with centrally symmetric homothetic parallel sections. They do not exhibit a balanced menu violating the weighted theorem; the planar stationary-chord theorem already rules that out. A different common scalar, or a payment retaining additional profile information, remains possible.

## 6. An exactly solvable nonaffine class: the source at the waist of a double cone

Let A,B>0 and take

    r(z)=1+z/A for -A<=z<=0,
    r(z)=1-z/B for 0<=z<=B.

Let D be any centered centrally symmetric m-body and K={(X,z):X in r(z)D}. The source is the waist center zero. If A=B, K is centrally symmetric, so every through-zero cap has exactly half the volume.

Suppose A!=B. Then every individually centroidal through-zero section has horizontal normal, in the sense that its cutting plane is z=0; no oblique section or vertical cutting plane has centroid zero. Consequently every balanced menu of such sections has mean cap fraction exactly1/2.

For the oblique claim, use the projective coordinate of Section1. The two reciprocal profile pieces are

    R(u)=1-u/A for u<=0,
    R(u)=1+u/B for u>=0,

and R-uR'=1. Hence

    w(u)=(1+u/B)^(-d-1),
    w(-u)=(1+u/A)^(-d-1), u>0.

If B>A, then w(u)>w(-u) for every u>0; if B<A the inequality reverses. For a nonzero horizontal cap coefficient c, let phi be the even projection density of D along c. The vertical section first moment has the sign of

    int_0^infinity u phi(u/|c|)[w(u)-w(-u)]du,

up to a positive scalar. It is nonzero, since phi is positive near zero. Thus an oblique section cannot have centroid zero.

For a vertical cutting plane c.X=0, its section has horizontal slices r(z)(D intersect c^perp). Its vertical centroid is the centroid of r(z)^(m-1) on [-A,B], namely

    (B-A)/(m+1),

which is nonzero. The formula also covers m=1, when the cutting section is a vertical segment and its midpoint is (B-A)/2. The horizontal plane z=0 has the centered section D. Its two cap orientations have the same section area and complementary volumes, so normal balance assigns equal total response weight to them. Their mean is1/2, as asserted.

The endpoint fibers at z=-A,B have zero volume but are ordinary apex points of the full-dimensional continuous body. All section and volume integrals above are taken in their proper dimensions; these endpoints cause no discarded mass.
